sections.h: Hezekiah's men and the book of Proverbs
sections.b: Proverbs 25:1 credits a collection of sayings to "the men of Hezekiah king of Judah", who "copied" them. The verb (he'tiqu) means moved or transferred: officials of the king's court carried older sayings of Solomon over into a new scroll. It is the only verse in the Bible that names a team of copyists and dates their work. It fits the picture Kings and Chronicles draw of Hezekiah as a reformer who restored worship "with the words of David and of Asaph" (2 Chronicles 29:30), and of a court with a secretary and a recorder (2 Kings 18:18). The Talmud took the note further and credited "Hezekiah and his company" with writing down Proverbs, Isaiah, the Song of Songs and Ecclesiastes (Bava Batra 15a). Chapters 25–29 of Proverbs are the result: sayings about kings and courtiers, fools and lazy men, friends and enemies, and the righteous and the wicked.

The fifth collection in Proverbs opens with its own heading (Proverbs 25:1) and runs to the end of chapter 29. Scholars usually divide it in two. Chapters 25–27 are full of pictures from nature and village life, often two images set side by side with no "like" or "so". Chapters 28–29 are mostly contrasts between the righteous and the wicked, with many sayings about rulers, the poor and the law. Several sayings repeat ones in Proverbs 10–22 (Proverbs 25:24 and 21:9; Proverbs 26:22 and 18:8; Proverbs 27:13 and 20:16; Proverbs 28:6 and 19:1), a sign that the collections were gathered separately. In the Greek translation these chapters stand in a different place, after parts of chapters 30 and 31, and the poem of the woman of strength follows directly after Proverbs 29:27.

sections.b: Proverbs tells the reader to feed the one who hates him when he is hungry and give him water when he is thirsty, "for you will be scooping up burning coals onto his head, / and the LORD will pay you back" (Proverbs 25:22). Readers have taken the coals as the burning shame that leads to repentance (Augustine and most Christian readers), as added judgment on an enemy who does not change, or as an allusion to an Egyptian rite in which a penitent carried coals on his head. Paul quotes the Greek of the saying in Romans 12:20, between "do not avenge yourselves" and "conquer evil with good", and leaves out the promised reward. With Jesus' command to love enemies (Matthew 5:44), it became a key text for Christian teaching on nonretaliation.

Proverbs 28:8 uses the law's pair of words for profit on a loan, neshekh ("bite") and tarbit ("increase"), as in Leviticus 25:36, and predicts that wealth grown this way will pass to "someone who is kind to the poor". The saying adds no new law but trusts that God will move unjust gains to others (compare Proverbs 13:22). Proverbs also warns again and again against guaranteeing another person's debt; Proverbs 27:13 repeats Proverbs 20:16, telling the lender to take the coat of a man who has backed a stranger's loan. In later history 28:8 was cited in the medieval church's case against usury and in Jewish law on lending, and the churches came to different positions on interest in commerce.

sections.b: "Rod and rebuke give wisdom, / but a boy left to run loose brings shame to his mother" (Proverbs 29:15). The saying joins the rod to spoken correction and names the goal, wisdom; its second line warns as much against neglect as it commends punishment. Proverbs 29:17 promises that a disciplined son will give his parent rest. Rabbinic law limited physical discipline (a teacher strikes "only with a shoelace", Bava Batra 21a; a father must not strike a grown son, Moed Katan 17a). Christians differ in how they apply the rod sayings, from measured spanking given in love (James Dobson) to readings that see the Bible moving toward gentler discipline (William Webb).

sections.b: The Hezekiah collection is full of sayings about speech: a word spoken at the right time is like golden apples in silver settings (Proverbs 25:11); patience can persuade a ruler, and a soft tongue breaks bone (Proverbs 25:15); a boaster who promises a gift and gives nothing is like clouds and wind with no rain (Proverbs 25:14). Chapter 26 ends with a gallery of harmful talkers: the meddler, the joker who deceives his neighbor, the gossip whose words go down like treats gulped down, the quarreler who feeds strife like wood on a fire, and the hater who hides behind smooth lips (Proverbs 26:17–28). The paired sayings on answering a fool (Proverbs 26:4–5) teach that even a true word needs the right time.

Four sayings in a row draw the lazy one as a cartoon (Proverbs 26:13–16). He will not go out because there is a lion in the streets; he turns on his bed like a door on its pivot; he buries his hand in the dish and is too tired to bring it back to his mouth; and he is wiser in his own eyes than seven people who can answer with good sense. Two of the sayings repeat earlier ones (Proverbs 22:13; Proverbs 19:24). Elsewhere in the collection the farmer who tills his soil has plenty of bread (Proverbs 28:19, repeating Proverbs 12:11), and the herdsman who knows his flock has food and clothing for his household (Proverbs 27:23–27).

sections.h: The dog and its vomit (2 Peter 2:22)
sections.b: 2 Peter closes its warning against false teachers by applying "the true proverb" to those who turn back after knowing Christ: a dog returns to its own vomit, and a washed sow goes back to the mud. The first saying comes from Proverbs 26:11, though 2 Peter does not use the wording of the Greek translation of Proverbs. The second is not in the Bible; a close relative appears in the Story of Ahiqar. Proverbs uses the dog for the fool who repeats his folly; 2 Peter applies it to those who leave the way of righteousness.

The sayings copied at Hezekiah's court have much to say about kings. The glory of kings is to search a matter out (Proverbs 25:2); remove the wicked from before the king and his throne will stand firm in righteousness (Proverbs 25:5); do not push yourself forward in the king's presence (Proverbs 25:6–7). Chapters 28–29, which Bruce Malchow called "a manual for future monarchs", warn that a wicked ruler over a poor people is a roaring lion (Proverbs 28:15), that a king who judges the poor faithfully will have a lasting throne (Proverbs 29:14), and that justice finally comes from the LORD (Proverbs 29:26). The herdsman's poem with its passing crown (Proverbs 27:23–27) may also have had a royal reader in view.

sections.b: Proverbs 28:13 sets two responses to wrongdoing side by side: hiding one's offenses, which does not prosper, and admitting and turning from them, which finds mercy. It joins confession and change, as Psalm 32 does, and rabbinic teaching on repentance cites it for the need to confess openly (Yoma 86b). Christians often read it with 1 John 1:9.
